summary.title: Laelii Capilupi Centones ex Virgilio (Rome: Dorico, 1555)

annotator.characterization: A single scholarly hand (two ink colours) that (a) corrected Dorico's pagination and text, (b) supplied at least one omitted Virgilian verse with its source-tag, and (c) collated the cento against Virgil, flagging seams — i.e. did by hand the apparatus work this edition now does by machine.

pages.heading: E. J. Kenney's bookplate
paragraphs: The front free endpaper, carrying the printed name-label bookplate “Edward John Kenney” and, beneath it in pencil, the note “Not in Adams.” From the library of E. J. Kenney (1924–2019), Kennedy Professor of Latin at Cambridge.

pages.editorial: The woodcut is not a printer's mark but the author's device: the wolf puns on the name Capilupi (“wolf-heads”) — a margin note in the book itself glosses it, “alludes to the wolf's head, emblem of the Capilupi family” — and the hourglass on the branch strikes a tempus-fugit note. That the book carries a proud authorial emblem yet no imprint at all — no place, printer, or date — is likely no accident: its centrepiece, the De vita monachorum, is an anti-monastic satire that went on the Index (1557), and the Capilupi centos have a history of suppressed and false imprints. The author signs the book with his wolf; the printer — Valerio Dorico of Rome — keeps his name off it.
paragraphs: LAELII CAPILVPI PATRITII MANTVANI CENTONES EX VIRGILIO.

[No imprint: the volume is sine notis — printed without place, printer, or date. It is attributed to the Roman press of Valerio Dorico (with his brother Luigi), c. 1555; the date is fixed by the Siege of Siena (1554–55), named in one of the printed margin notes.]
paragraphs_en: Centos out of Virgil, by Laelius Capilupi, patrician of Mantua.

pages.heading: IOACHIMO BELAIO ANTONIVS POSSEVINVS MANTVANVS S. P. D.
pages.editorial: Dedicatee: Joachim du Bellay (Latin Ioachimus Bellaius, 1522–1560), poet of the Pléiade, then living in Rome. The address is pointed: the author of the Deffence et illustration de la langue françoyse (1549) — the manifesto of poetic originality — is here presented a Virgilian cento, the purest imitation. And du Bellay was no stranger to Capilupi: he drew on him in L'Olive. See the launch essay, “The Machinery of Originality,” on reuse and invention in a book made entirely of Virgil.
paragraphs: Omnium omnino qui aliquid in lucem redeunt duo genera sunt, alterum eorum à quibus res ipsæ inueniuntur, alterum illorum, qui quod dicturi sunt aliunde assumunt: atque hoc genus in duas parteis rursus distributum est, nam aut qui ab alijs res accipiunt, eas suis uerbis exponunt, aut ad sententias suas aliorum uerba transferunt, atque traducunt, quod quidem pertinet ad eos, qui Centones conscribunt, quo in genere ita mirabilis fuit Lælius Capilupus, ut facilè omnium expectationem uicerit, ac superarit. Nam cum plerumque de rebus ab antiquorum ætate remotissimis agat, eas tamen ita Virgily carminibus tractat, atque complectitur, ut ne ipsum quidem Poëtam supra potuisse existimem. Nam & in dispositione sententiarum, & ordine, & in coniungendis, ac quasi conglutinandis uersibus, qui in Virgilij libris maximo interuallo inter se disiuncti sunt, illud est omnium iudicio consecutus, ut perpetuum potius, et continens scriptum, quàm undique collectum, & comportatum uideatur: in quo uiri illius memoriam, & acre iudicium soleo sæpe admirari, qui res tam dispersas in unum locum cogat, easq; ita collocet, ut media primis, extremis prima respondeant. ac ut perfectus fictor, qui ex diuersissimis lapidibus opus egregium fingit, emblemateq; componit, sic ille ex omnibus Virgilij locis, quæ ad suam sententiam in primis facerent optima quæq; excerpsit, atque libauit, unumq; hoc corpus confecit. Scio autem nonnullos ad hoc scribendi genus se contulisse, in quorum numero apud Græcos fuit
paragraphs_en: Of all those whatsoever who bring something forth into the light, there are two kinds: the one comprising those by whom the matters themselves are invented, the other comprising those who take up elsewhere what they mean to say. And this latter kind is in turn divided into two parts: for either they take material from others and set it forth in their own words, or they transfer and adapt the words of others to their own purposes — which indeed applies to those who compose Centos. In this genre Lelio Capilupi was so remarkable that he easily surpassed and exceeded everyone's expectation. For although he deals for the most part with matters most remote from the age of the ancients, he nevertheless treats and encompasses them by means of Virgil's verses so skillfully that I do not think even the Poet himself could have done better. For both in the arrangement and order of the thoughts, and in joining together and, as it were, cementing the verses — which in Virgil's own books are separated from one another by the greatest distance — he has achieved this, in the judgment of all, that the work seems rather a continuous and unbroken composition than one gathered and assembled from every quarter. In this I am often accustomed to admire that man's memory and keen judgment, who could gather matters so scattered into a single place and arrange them in such a way that the middle answers to the beginning, and the beginning to the end. And just as a consummate craftsman, who out of the most varied stones fashions an outstanding work and composes it as a mosaic, so he, out of all the passages of Virgil, culled and gathered whatever was best and most suited above all to his own purpose, and from them fashioned this one body of work. I know, moreover, that a number of others have applied themselves to this kind of writing; among their number, among the Greeks, was

pages.editorial: “Tum summo illi Cardinali” (“and to that most eminent Cardinal”): Cardinal Jean du Bellay, kinsman and patron of the dedicatee Joachim du Bellay, whom Joachim served in Rome. The dedication reaches the poet’s powerful cousin through the poet. See the essay “The Machinery of Originality.”
paragraphs: Eudocia ,apud Latinos Proba Falconia, & Ausonius, sed quantum in eo profecerint, aliorum sit iudicium. Illud quidem nec dubitans affirmauerim Lælio non modo in hac re non præstantiores fuisse, sed uix fortasse pares. Nam ut de Ausonio loquar, cum hic de rebus ipsis ageret, facilè illi fuit ad id quod sentiret Poetæ carmina accommodare, longè enim alia notio subijcitur his scriptis, atque illa, quæ Virgilianis subiecta est.

Cum igitur hos Centones sæpissimè legissem, prospiceremq; hunc librum si ederetur iucundissimum omnibus, & utilissimum fore, Lælium rogaui qui mihi potestatem daret ut eum emitterem, quod cum ille ut solet, humanissimè mihi permisisset, nihil mihi antiquius, aut longius fuit, quam ut in manus hominum exiret, etenim præter maximum & uberrimum fructum, quem ex eo quiuis percepturus fuisset, non mediocre commodum me adepturum sciebam, neque.n.dulcius quidquam aut iucundius mihi accidere poterat, quam ut illius scripta proferrentur, quem præterquam quod cum eo summis beneuolentiæ & amicitiæ uinculis sum coniunctus, [printed word struck through in ink, illegible] non modo ob charitatem patriæ quæ illi cum multis est cõmunis , uerùm etiam ob singulares eius uirtutes summo semper amore sum prosecutus. Præterea illud mihi maximo usui futurum uidebam, cum ob hanc causam aditum mihi ad te patefacerem, gratiamq; tuam quodammodo aucuparer. Tu enim is es, qui & summa uirtute præditus, & omnibus literarum studijs ornatissimus Læly Capilupi scripta es adeo admiratus, ut cum ne illum quidem uirum de facie cognosceres, mirificè tamen amares & coleres, quod cum illius ingenio, tum tuæ humanitati & animo ad studia propenso tribuitur. Adeo in humanis animis studia paria possunt, quæ quo sunt liberaliora, eò magis homines inter se quibusdam uinculis deuinciunt, & obstringunt. Quibus rationibus adductus statui hunc librum ad te mittere, quod scirem apud neminem in loco meliore aut honestiore esse posse. Cum enim semper otium, & tempus in discendo contriueris, tum summo illi Cardinali
paragraphs_en: Eudocia, and among the Latins Proba Falconia and Ausonius — but how far they succeeded in this, let others judge. This much, indeed, I would affirm without hesitation: that in this respect they were not only not superior to Laelius, but perhaps scarcely even his equals. For, to speak of Ausonius, since he was dealing with the very subject matter itself, it was easy for him to fit the Poet's verses to what he meant; for a far different sense is imposed upon these writings than that which underlies the Virgilian lines themselves.

Since, then, I had read these Centos very often, and foresaw that this book, if published, would be most delightful and most useful to everyone, I asked Laelius to grant me leave to bring it out; and when he, as is his custom, most courteously permitted me this, nothing was dearer to me or more pressing than that it should come into men's hands. For besides the very great and abundant benefit that anyone at all would derive from it, I knew that I myself would gain no small advantage; nor indeed could anything sweeter or more pleasant befall me than that the writings of that man should be brought forth — a man to whom, quite apart from the fact that I am joined to him by the closest ties of goodwill and friendship, [omitted: struck-through word, illegible] I have always been devoted with the deepest love, not only on account of our shared love of our homeland, which he shares with many others, but also on account of his singular virtues. Moreover, I saw that this would be of the greatest use to me, since by this occasion I might open a way of approach to you, and in some measure court your favor. For you are one who, endowed with the highest virtue and most accomplished in every literary pursuit, so admired the writings of Laelius Capilupi that, although you did not even know the man by sight, you nevertheless loved and cherished him wonderfully — a thing owed both to his genius and to your own courtesy and disposition inclined toward learning. So great is the power that shared pursuits have over human minds, that the more liberal they are, the more they bind and constrain men to one another by certain ties. Moved by these considerations, I resolved to send this book to you, since I knew that with no one could it find a better or more honorable place. For as you have always spent your leisure and your time in learning, so too [you have always been devoted] to that most eminent Cardinal—

paragraphs_en: ...are joined by blood — a man in whom one could not easily judge whether his character was made illustrious and adorned by his learning, or his learning by his character. And for my part, I trust that my design will meet with your approval, and that you will receive this gift with the courtesy you have always shown, since it proceeds, certainly, from a mind most devoted to you, and is offered to you. It remains only that you love us, and — since you have taken up the patronage of letters with such a ready spirit — that you will defend and protect this book from the slanders of its detractors. Farewell.

pages.heading: L. FVLVIVS· VRSINVS· LECTORI S.
pages.editorial: Heading: “L. Fulvius Ursinus Lectori S.” = Fulvio Orsini to the reader, greetings. Orsini’s closing address, telling how Antonio Possevino wrung the centos from Capilupi by near-daily importunity and brought them to press. A paratext of this 1555 Roman edition. See the essay “The Machinery of Originality.”
paragraphs:
NTONIVS Posseuinus, iuuenis cum
morum suauitate & elegantia, tum etiam
eruditione incredibili, hosce Lælij Capilu-
pi Centones miro artificio è Virgilianis
uersibus concinnatos, ab auctore quotidia-
nis propè conuicijs extortos ediderat. Cum autem Lælius
pro singulari sua in uiros bonarum artium & literarum stu-
diosos beneuolentia, nonnulla mihi illorum exemplaria litte-

paragraphs_en: Antonio Possevino, a young man distinguished not only by sweetness and elegance of character but also by incredible learning, had published these Centos of Laelius Capilupi — marvelously fashioned out of Virgilian verses — which had been wrung from their author by almost daily importunities. Since Laelius, out of his singular goodwill toward men devoted to the good arts and to letters, had given me a number of copies of them to be bestowed, at my own discretion, upon men of letters, I judged Benedictus Aegius of Spoleto — whose learning and humanity are, I think, unknown to no one — not unworthy of so great a gift. He indeed, once he had read through the work, composed the distich set out above, fitted to this subject, and gave it to me to read; and when I had committed it to memory and, a little later, happened to meet Capilupo, I recited it to him. He at once, in return for the distich — such being his extraordinary memory, judgment, wisdom, and generosity, imitating the most fertile soil — composed a whole Cento in praise of B. Aegius in the space of scarcely an hour and a half. Wherefore, thinking I would be doing something worthwhile, I have willingly and gladly, on behalf of Antonio Possevino — by far the most devoted to me of all men, and to whom, because he was away,
